hackernews.author: isuruwijesiri
hackernews.body:
Harness Engineering 101: The LLM is the brain, the harness is the body
When i wrote my own harness, i didn't rely on what other agents do, but rather sat down and considered how i can solve the issues that i have when using other agents. And tbh, for alot of problems there are rather "simple" fixes - each comes with a cost tho. For me it was accepting to run more infer... Harness optimization is essential. Doesn’t matter how smart the model is if the tools you give it are ineffective, or the task is under defined. It needs invent the solution from first principles every time.
We did a harness optimization on Jev. Raw it was no where near as good as deekseek, but opti... Better analogy:
    The LLM is the oven, the harness is the kitchen.  You prep all your ingredients and put it into the oven (flour, water, salt, sugar).  It transforms those inputs into a finished product (cake, loaf of bread).

comment_insights: When i wrote my own harness, i didn't rely on what other agents do, but rather sat down and considered how i can solve the issues that i have when using other agents
Harness optimization is essential
Better analogy:
Instead of reading AI-slop explanations full of creaky metaphors, I'd advise you to just build your own basic coding harness from scratch
LLM is to harness as Krang is to his android body.

hackernews.author: CharlesW
hackernews.body:
The engineering that allows articulated buses to bend
I like watching the other half of the bus while riding these. It's a cool effect, seeing the whole "room" oscillate through the "doorway", while I feel like I'm standing still.
Edit: The article has a video of this effect near the bottom. Just 2 days ago: one of these buses had an accident that left the front part twisted 180 degrees in relation to the rear: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=flbaRmGKzPY
The Munich bus-trailer in action: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4IUE-yA8R1A When I got to where they explained the benefits of having the engine at the very back and the instability of having the back part push the front, I tried to guess how they solved it. I guessed a fancy drive shaft with universal joints so the engine in the back half could drive wheels in the front ha...

comment_insights: I like watching the other half of the bus while riding these
Just 2 days ago: one of these buses had an accident that left the front part twisted 180 degrees in relation to the rear: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=flbaRmGKzPY
When I got to where they explained the benefits of having the engine at the very back and the instability of having the back part push the front, I tried to guess how they solved it
This article's byline features one of the most magnificent cases of nominative determinism I've ever seen
Omg! My whole life I thought that the rear engine articulated buses transferred the torque to the middle axle (the rear axle of the front “bus”)!
